# Tobit Chapter 13 — Disagreement Log
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Date:** 2026-03-17

---

## Summary
Chapter 13 is the psalm of Tobit — the book's sole sustained lyric passage. Translating poetry introduces heightened disagreement because choices of register, line-break, and interpretive expansion all diverge significantly between a literal and dynamic approach. 12 divergences were logged across the 18 verses.

---

## Disagreement Table

| Verse | Issue | EMET | LOGOS | PNEUMA | Resolution |
|-------|-------|------|-------|--------|------------|
| 13:1 | Character of the writing | "wrote a-prayer of rejoicing" | "wrote a prayer of rejoicing" | "poured out this song of praise" | **LOGOS** — "prayer of rejoicing" (*proseuchēn eis agalliasma*) is the Greek compound; PNEUMA's "song" is interpretive, though not wrong given the hymnic content |
| 13:2 | Realm of death | "leads-down to-Hades" | "leads down to Hades" | "sends down to the grave" | **LOGOS/EMET** — *hadou* = Hades specifically; translating as "grave" (*sheol*) flattens a deliberate Greek theological concept |
| 13:2 | Grip of God | "none who-will-escape from his-hand" | "no one who can escape from his hand" | "No one slips from his grip" | **LOGOS** — PNEUMA is vivid but registers as too colloquial for a hymn; LOGOS's "can escape" is fluid |
| 13:4 | Universal scope | "every living [being]" (bracketed) | "every living creature" | "every living soul" | **LOGOS** — "creature" is the natural English idiom for *pasa psychē zōsa*; "soul" in PNEUMA is fine but edges toward anthropocentrism |
| 13:5 | Restoration promise | "will-gather-us from all the-nations" | "gather us from all the nations" | "gathers us home" | **LOGOS** — "home" is a reasonable inference but not in the Greek; consensus keeps the neutral direction |
| 13:6 | Divine uncertainty hedge | "who-knows, perhaps he-will-show-favor and he-will-have-mercy" | "who knows — perhaps he will look with favor on you and show you mercy" | "Who knows — perhaps he will be gracious, perhaps he will have mercy on you" | **LOGOS** — all three capture the rhetorical hedge (*tis oiden*); LOGOS flows best; PNEUMA's repetition of "perhaps" is expressive but slightly redundant |
| 13:9 | "sons" vs. "children" | "works of your-sons" | "deeds of your children" | "what your children have done" | **LOGOS** — "children" (*huiōn*) is gender-inclusive in context; "sons" in EMET is technically accurate to the Greek but misrepresents the intended scope |
| 13:10 | Compassion for the afflicted | "may-love in-you those-who-are-miserable" | "cherish in you those who are wretched" | "hold the broken ones close" | **LOGOS** — *agapēsē* = "love/cherish"; "wretched" for *kakōs echontas* is more precise than "miserable" or "broken" |
| 13:11 | Generational worship | "Generations of generations will-offer in-you joyful-worship" | "Generations of generations will offer joyful worship in you" | "Generation after generation will come to worship you with joy" | **LOGOS** — "Generations of generations" (*genea geneōn*) is a Hebraism worth preserving; PNEUMA's "come to worship" adds movement |
| 13:12 | Curse register | hyphenated construct clusters | declarative sentences "Cursed are all who..." | subjunctive "Cursed be anyone who..." | **LOGOS** — declarative present is most appropriate for liturgical curse/beatitude formula; EMET's hyphens read awkwardly in poetry |
| 13:16 | Gold description | "with-pure gold" | "with pure gold" | "gleaming gold, pure and bright" | **LOGOS** — *chrysiō katharō* = "pure gold"; PNEUMA's "gleaming" and "bright" are elaborations not in the Greek |
| 13:17 | Hallelujah | "will-cry-out 'Hallelujah'" | "will cry out 'Hallelujah'" | "will ring with 'Hallelujah!'" | **LOGOS** — "ring" in PNEUMA is a nice acoustic image but *boēsontai* = "will cry/shout" is the actual word |

---

## Thematic Notes

**The Jerusalem address (vv. 9–17):** The second half of the psalm shifts from personal to civic address — Tobit speaks directly to the city of Jerusalem in apostrophe. This is the formal feature that most clearly distinguishes the psalm as a literary composition, not merely a prayer. PNEUMA handles the apostrophe well; LOGOS is cleaner for the gemstone catalog.

**Gemstone intertextuality:** The jewel list in vv. 16–17 consciously echoes Isaiah 54:11–12 ("I will set your stones in antimony... your foundations with sapphires... your gates with carbuncles and all your wall with precious stones") and anticipates Revelation 21:18–21. This is the author's most explicit connection to the prophetic tradition of New Jerusalem. All three agents recognize this but only EMET and LOGOS explicitly name "stone of Ophir" as a preserved proper noun.

**Verse 6 — the center of the psalm:** The conditional "If you turn to him... then he will turn to you" is the theological axis. It is not merely poetic — it is covenantal. The language echoes the Deuteronomic call-to-return (*shub*) throughout Deuteronomy and Jeremiah. PNEUMA renders this beautifully but slightly overwrites; LOGOS and EMET preserve the covenant structure intact.

**Disagreement count: 12**

— SOPHIA
